periods.title: Nizwa Fort & Friday Goat Market
periods.text: Start early at Nizwa Fort, Oman's most visited monument, built in the 1650s by Sultan Bin Saif Al Ya'rubi. The massive circular tower (40m diameter, 30m tall) offers panoramic views over the date palm oasis and Al Hajar mountains. Entry is free. If visiting on Friday, don't miss the Livestock Market (6–9am) where Omani traders in dishdashas haggle over goats and cattle in a chaotic, photogenic ring.
periods.tip: The Friday goat market peaks at 7am and winds down by 9am. Arrive early, as it's one of the most authentic experiences in Oman.

periods.title: Nizwa Souq: Silver, Khanjars & Dates
periods.text: Adjacent to the fort, Nizwa Souq is one of the oldest and most traditional in Oman. The silver section sells Omani khanjars (ornate curved daggers, from OMR 15 for simple ones to OMR 500+ for antiques), silver jewellery, and frankincense burners. The date section has dozens of varieties. Try khalas (sweet, caramel-like) and fardh (dried, chewy). Lunch at a local restaurant, where shuwa-style lamb with rice costs OMR 2–3.
periods.tip: Khanjar prices vary hugely, as the silver content and craftsmanship determine value. Ask the shopkeeper to explain the differences.

periods.title: Birkat Al Mouz & Sunset
periods.text: Drive 25 minutes north to Birkat Al Mouz, an ancient terraced settlement at the foot of Jebel Akhdar with a crumbling mud-brick village, restored falaj (irrigation channel), and vast date palm plantation. Walk the falaj path through the oasis as the late afternoon light turns the mountains golden. Return to Nizwa for dinner and try mashuai (spit-roasted kingfish with lemon rice) at a local restaurant.
periods.tip: Birkat Al Mouz is free and rarely crowded. The abandoned village above the oasis is safe to explore but watch your step.

periods.title: Nizwa Fort & Livestock Market
periods.text: Start at Nizwa Fort, the largest fort in the Arabian Peninsula, built in the 1650s with a massive drum tower offering 360-degree views over the date palm oasis and Al Hajar mountains. Entry is free, and the museum inside explains Omani history, weaponry, and daily life. If it's Friday, arrive by 6:30am for the Livestock Market, where Omani traders in white dishdashas haggle over goats in a circular ring.
periods.tip: Friday is the absolute best day to visit Nizwa. The goat market alone is worth planning your trip around.

periods.title: Nizwa Souq
periods.text: Adjacent to the fort, this traditional souq is a labyrinth of silver workshops, khanjar (dagger) stalls, pottery, frankincense, and spices. The date section is extraordinary, with dozens of varieties laid out in huge baskets. Try khalas and fardh. Lunch at Bin Ateeq restaurant for traditional Omani food served on the floor: shuwa lamb, harees, and luqaimat (sweet dumplings) for OMR 3–5.
periods.tip: The souq is busiest (and best) on Friday mornings. Weekday afternoons are quieter for shopping without the crowds.

periods.title: Birkat Al Mouz & Sunset
periods.text: Drive 25 minutes north to Birkat Al Mouz, a stunning terraced settlement at the base of Jebel Akhdar. Walk the ancient falaj irrigation channel through the date palm plantation, explore the crumbling mud-brick village above, and watch the sunset turn the mountains from brown to gold to purple.
periods.tip: Birkat Al Mouz is free and uncrowded. The abandoned village above is atmospheric but uneven, so wear sturdy shoes.

periods.title: Drive to Jebel Akhdar
periods.text: Rent a 4x4 (required by law, with a police checkpoint at the base) and drive up the winding road to Jebel Akhdar (Green Mountain, 2,000m). The road climbs through dramatic gorges and terraced villages. Stop at Diana's Point viewpoint for a vertigo-inducing look down a 1,000m canyon. The mountain air is noticeably cooler than Nizwa below.
periods.tip: A basic 4x4 rental is OMR 25–35/day. You cannot pass the checkpoint without one, no exceptions.

periods.title: Terraced Villages & Rose Water
periods.text: Explore the hanging villages of Al Ayn and Al Aqr, stone houses perched on cliff edges above terraced gardens of pomegranates, walnuts, and damask roses. If visiting March–April, the rose harvest is in full bloom and families distill rose water in copper pots. Buy a bottle (OMR 2–5), as the scent is intoxicating. Walk the village-to-village path along the cliff edge.
periods.tip: Rose water distilling season is late March to mid-April. Outside this period, the villages are still beautiful but without the harvest activity.

periods.title: Sunset on the Mountain
periods.text: Drive to the viewing platform near Anantara resort for the best sunset vista, when the canyon below turns crimson as the light fades. Dinner at a local guesthouse in Sayq (OMR 5–8 for a home-cooked meal) or bring supplies for a mountain picnic. Return to Nizwa after dark, as the stargazing during the descent is spectacular.
periods.tip: Bring layers. Jebel Akhdar drops to 5–10°C in winter evenings, even when Nizwa is 25°C.

periods.title: Bahla Fort & Jabrin Castle
periods.text: Drive 40 minutes west to Bahla Fort (UNESCO, free), a vast, partially restored mud-brick fortress with 12km of walls surrounding the old town. Then continue to Jabrin Castle (OMR 0.5), more refined than Nizwa Fort, with painted ceilings, sun and moon rooms, and a falaj running through the interior. It was both a fortress and a centre of Islamic learning.
periods.tip: Jabrin Castle is the most architecturally interesting fort in Oman, so don't skip it. The painted ceilings in the upper rooms are exceptional.

periods.title: Tanuf Ruins & Falaj Daris
periods.text: Visit the bombed ruins of Tanuf, a village destroyed during the Jebel Akhdar War in the 1950s and left as a memorial. The crumbling walls against the mountain backdrop are hauntingly photogenic. Nearby, Falaj Daris (UNESCO) is Oman's largest irrigation channel, a 3,000-year-old engineering marvel still watering Nizwa's date plantations. Walk along the channel through the oasis.
periods.tip: Tanuf has a natural spring pool nearby where locals swim, a refreshing stop in the heat.

periods.title: Farewell Dinner in Nizwa
periods.text: Final evening in Nizwa's souq area, where the old town is atmospheric at night with warm lighting and fewer tourists. Dinner at a traditional Omani restaurant: try mashuai (spit-roasted kingfish) or a lamb shuwa platter. Pick up last-minute frankincense, halwa (Omani sweet), or silver from the souq.
periods.tip: Omani halwa (a rose water and saffron sweet) makes an excellent gift, sold in decorative tins at the souq for OMR 1–3.

periods.title: Nizwa Fort & Livestock Market
periods.text: Start at Nizwa Fort, the largest fort in the Arabian Peninsula, built in the 1650s with a massive drum tower and free entry. If it's Friday, arrive by 6:30am for the Livestock Market where Omani traders haggle over goats in a circular ring.
periods.tip: Plan your trip to include a Friday in Nizwa, as the goat market is unmissable.

periods.title: Nizwa Souq
periods.text: Explore the traditional souq for silver workshops, khanjar stalls, pottery, frankincense, and date varieties. Lunch at Bin Ateeq restaurant: shuwa lamb, harees, and luqaimat for OMR 3–5.
periods.tip: Weekday afternoons are quieter for shopping. The souq closes around 9pm.

periods.title: Birkat Al Mouz
periods.text: Drive to Birkat Al Mouz, a terraced settlement with falaj irrigation channels, a crumbling mud-brick village, and date palm plantations at the foot of Jebel Akhdar. Walk the falaj path at sunset.
periods.tip: Free and uncrowded. The abandoned village above is atmospheric but wear sturdy shoes.

periods.title: Drive to Jebel Akhdar
periods.text: Rent a 4x4 (required, with a police checkpoint at the base) and drive up to Jebel Akhdar (2,000m). Stop at Diana's Point for a vertigo-inducing 1,000m canyon view.
periods.tip: Basic 4x4 rental is OMR 25–35/day. You cannot pass the checkpoint without one.

periods.title: Terraced Villages & Rose Water
periods.text: Explore Al Ayn and Al Aqr, stone houses above terraced gardens of pomegranates, walnuts, and damask roses. In March–April, watch families distill rose water. Walk the cliff-edge village path.
periods.tip: Rose water distilling season is late March to mid-April.

periods.title: Mountain Sunset
periods.text: Watch sunset from the canyon viewpoints as the gorge turns crimson. Dinner at a local guesthouse in Sayq (OMR 5–8). Return to Nizwa under stars.
periods.tip: Bring layers. Jebel Akhdar drops to 5–10°C in winter evenings.

periods.title: Bahla Fort
periods.text: Drive 40 minutes to Bahla Fort (UNESCO, free), a vast mud-brick fortress with 12km of walls. The old town of Bahla is known for pottery, so watch artisans at work in the workshops near the fort.
periods.tip: Bahla is also known as Oman's "magic town". Ask locals about the folklore, it's fascinating.

periods.title: Jabrin Castle
periods.text: Jabrin Castle (OMR 0.5) is the most refined fort in Oman, with painted ceilings, sun and moon rooms, and a falaj running through the interior. It doubled as a centre of Islamic learning. Allow 1.5 hours.
periods.tip: The painted ceilings in the upper rooms are exceptional, so bring a phone flashlight to see the details.

periods.title: Tanuf Ruins
periods.text: Visit the bombed ruins of Tanuf, destroyed in the 1950s Jebel Akhdar War and left as a memorial. The crumbling walls against the mountains are haunting. Nearby is a natural spring pool where locals swim.
periods.tip: Combine Tanuf with a swim at the spring, refreshing after a day of fort-hopping.

periods.title: Drive to Jebel Shams
periods.text: Drive 90 minutes from Nizwa to Jebel Shams, Oman's highest peak (3,009m) and its "Grand Canyon." The road climbs through desert landscapes into dramatic mountain terrain. Stop at the abandoned village of Ghul overlooking Wadi Ghul, a 1,000m-deep gorge.
periods.tip: 4x4 recommended but not strictly required on the paved road. The last 2km to the viewpoint is rough gravel.

periods.title: Balcony Walk Hike
periods.text: The Balcony Walk (W6 trail) is one of Oman's best hikes, a 6km out-and-back path along a narrow ledge carved into the cliff face with 1,000m drops to the wadi below. The trail passes the abandoned village of As Sab and ends at a seasonal waterfall. Allow 3–4 hours round trip.
periods.tip: Not for those with vertigo. The trail is exposed but well-trodden. Bring 2+ litres of water.

periods.title: Canyon Sunset & Return
periods.text: Watch sunset from the canyon rim as the gorge turns from gold to purple and shadows deepen. The drive back to Nizwa takes 90 minutes. Stop at Al Hamra on the way, a 400-year-old mud-brick town that's one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements in Oman.
periods.tip: Al Hamra's old town is free to explore and beautifully lit at dusk. Bait Al Safah museum demonstrates traditional Omani life.

periods.title: Drive to Wadi Bani Khalid
periods.text: Drive 2 hours east to Wadi Bani Khalid, Oman's most accessible wadi with year-round turquoise pools surrounded by palm trees and limestone cliffs. The first pool is easy to reach (10-minute walk from parking). Swim in the crystal-clear water and explore the cave at the upstream end.
periods.tip: Arrive before 10am to have the pools to yourself. By noon, local families and tour groups arrive.

periods.title: Upper Pools & Village
periods.text: Hike upstream to the second and third pools, less crowded and more dramatic. The cave at pool three is 200m deep with stalactites and a cold stream. Walk through the traditional village at the wadi entrance for date gardens, falaj channels, and friendly residents. Lunch at the wadi cafe (OMR 2–4).
periods.tip: Bring water shoes, as the rocks between pools are slippery. A waterproof phone pouch is worth having.

periods.title: Return via Al Mudayrib
periods.text: Return to Nizwa via Al Mudayrib, a fortified village with watchtowers and traditional houses. If it's dates season (June–August), roadside vendors sell fresh dates for OMR 0.5/kg. Dinner in Nizwa at a local restaurant.
periods.tip: The drive back takes 2 hours. Fill up on fuel before leaving Wadi Bani Khalid, as there are no stations for 60km.

periods.title: Al Hamra Old Town
periods.text: Drive 45 minutes to Al Hamra, a 400-year-old mud-brick town and one of Oman's oldest settlements. Walk through the crumbling lanes of the old quarter. Visit Bait Al Safah (OMR 1), a living museum where women demonstrate traditional bread-making, coffee-roasting, and date-pressing.
periods.tip: Al Hamra's old town is best in the morning light. The mud buildings glow golden before 10am.

periods.title: Misfat Al Abriyyin
periods.text: Continue 15 minutes to Misfat Al Abriyyin, a stunning mountain village of stone houses cascading down a cliff above terraced gardens. Walk the winding alleys and falaj channels. The village guesthouse serves traditional lunch on a terrace overlooking the valley (OMR 3–5). The swimming pool at the base of the village is fed by mountain springs.
periods.tip: Misfat is tiny, so 2 hours is enough. But it's one of the most photogenic villages in Oman.

periods.title: Return to Nizwa
periods.text: Drive back through the mountain villages. Stop at a roadside honey seller, as Omani mountain honey (OMR 5–15 per jar) is prized locally. Final evening in Nizwa, where the fort is beautifully illuminated at night.
periods.tip: Omani mountain honey is expensive but exceptional. The dark, thick variety from Jebel Akhdar is the most prized.

periods.title: Falaj Daris & Date Plantations
periods.text: Visit Falaj Daris (UNESCO), Oman's largest irrigation channel, part of a 3,000-year-old system still watering Nizwa's plantations. Walk along the channel through the date palm oasis. The park around the falaj has shaded seating and is a peaceful spot for a final morning.
periods.tip: The falaj system is an engineering marvel. Water is distributed by a complex rotation system among farming families.

periods.title: Last Shopping & Souq Visit
periods.text: Final visit to Nizwa Souq for souvenirs: frankincense (luban, OMR 1–5), silver jewellery, halwa (Omani rose-water sweet, OMR 1–3 per tin), and dates. The pottery section sells traditional Omani coffee pots and incense burners.
periods.tip: Frankincense makes an excellent lightweight gift. The best quality is Hojari grade, pale, translucent pieces.

periods.title: Departure
periods.text: Nizwa is 1.5 hours from Muscat International Airport. The drive passes through dramatic mountain gorges and descends to the coast. If departing later, spend the afternoon at the Royal Opera House district in Muscat or the Mutrah Corniche for a final sunset.
periods.tip: The Nizwa–Muscat highway is excellent. Allow 2 hours with airport buffer time.

budgetTips.title: Free forts
budgetTips.text: Nizwa Fort, Bahla Fort, and many smaller forts are free. Jabrin Castle is just OMR 0.5. Oman's heritage sites are remarkably affordable.

budgetTips.title: Eat local
budgetTips.text: Traditional restaurants serve full meals (rice, meat, sides) for OMR 1.5–3. Roadside shawarma and falafel for OMR 0.3–0.5. The souq has cheap dates and fruit.

budgetTips.title: Camp for free
budgetTips.text: Wild camping is legal throughout Oman. Jebel Shams, Jebel Akhdar, and wadi mouths are popular free camping spots. Bring a tent or sleep under the stars.

budgetTips.title: Share 4x4 costs
budgetTips.text: Jebel Akhdar and Jebel Shams require 4x4s (OMR 25–35/day). Split with fellow travellers, as many hostels organise shared trips.

budgetTips.title: Fuel is cheap
budgetTips.text: Petrol costs around OMR 0.21/litre (~$0.55). Driving around Oman is far cheaper than in Europe. Fill up in towns, as stations are sparse in mountains.

budgetTips.title: Water is free
budgetTips.text: Most mosques have free water taps outside. Refill your bottle at mosques, petrol stations, and restaurants. Bottled water costs OMR 0.1–0.2 if needed.

budgetBreakdown.notes: Shared transport → rental car → 4x4 with driver
Free forts & wadis → guided tours → adventure activities

practicalInfo.title: Visa & Entry
items: Most nationalities get visa on arrival (OMR 20 for 30 days). Some qualify for free entry, so check before travelling
Passport must be valid for 6+ months. Oman is strict about this at immigration
Nizwa is 1.5 hours from Muscat International Airport via an excellent highway

practicalInfo.title: Health & Safety
items: No vaccinations required. Tap water is safe in cities but stick to bottled in rural areas
Oman is one of the safest countries in the world, and violent crime is virtually non-existent
Heat is the main risk: 45°C+ in summer (Jun–Sep). Avoid outdoor activities midday in summer

practicalInfo.title: Getting Around
items: A rental car is essential for exploring around Nizwa, as public transport is minimal outside Muscat
Standard car (OMR 10–15/day) is fine for paved roads. 4x4 (OMR 25–35/day) required for Jebel Akhdar and off-road wadis
Drive on the right. Roads are excellent. Speed cameras are everywhere and fines are steep

practicalInfo.title: Connectivity
items: Tourist SIM: Omantel or Ooredoo, OMR 5–10 for 10GB. Available at Muscat airport
WiFi is generally good in hotels. Mountain areas have patchy coverage
Download offline maps. GPS signal is fine but mobile data drops out in wadis and mountains

practicalInfo.title: Money
items: Omani Rial is pegged near the USD (1 OMR ≈ 2.60 USD). It's one of the highest-value currencies in the world
Cards accepted at hotels and larger restaurants. Cash essential for souqs, small eateries, and fuel stations
ATMs available in Nizwa centre. Carry enough cash for day trips, as there are no ATMs in mountains or wadis

practicalInfo.title: Packing Tips
items: Conservative dress: cover shoulders and knees. Long, loose, breathable clothing is ideal for heat and culture
Sturdy hiking shoes for wadis and mountains. Water shoes for wadi pools. Sandals for towns
Headscarf for women visiting mosques. Sun hat, SPF 50+ sunscreen, and at least 2L water capacity

culturalTips.title: Dress Code
culturalTips.text: Oman is conservative. Cover shoulders and knees at all times in public. Swimwear is only for wadi pools and hotel pools. Women don't need to cover their hair except in mosques.

culturalTips.title: Mosque Etiquette
culturalTips.text: Non-Muslims generally cannot enter mosques in Oman (Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque in Muscat is the exception). Respect prayer times, as shops and restaurants may close briefly.

culturalTips.title: Photography
culturalTips.text: Always ask before photographing Omanis, especially women. Never photograph military or government buildings. The Friday goat market is fair game, as traders are used to cameras.

culturalTips.title: Hospitality
culturalTips.text: Omanis are famously hospitable. If invited for coffee and dates, accepting is polite. Remove shoes before entering homes. Use your right hand for eating and greeting.

culturalTips.title: Driving Culture
culturalTips.text: Omanis drive fast but politely. Flash headlights mean "I'm coming through" on mountain roads. Move aside for faster vehicles. Don't honk unnecessarily, as it's considered rude.
